Testified
TES-ti-fide
v. (past t. and past part.)
From Latin testificari, to bear witness, from testis (a witness) and facere (to make). Webster 1828: bore witness to; affirmed or declared solemnly; gave evidence. The word is legal before it is religious: a testis is a man in court whose word is evidence.

Biblical Definition

Testified is courtroom language pressed into the service of the gospel, and the New Testament never treats preaching as opinion offered but as evidence given. Paul at Corinth is described in exactly these terms: Paul was pressed in the spirit, and testified to the Jews that Jesus was Christ (Acts 18:5). The content is a fact about a Person, not a philosophy, and Paul is under pressure to state it. The summary of his whole ministry among Jews and Greeks alike is the same word: Testifying both to the Jews, and also to the Greeks, repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ (Acts 20:21) — one message, two directions, both parts required. Testimony also runs backward through the prophets, and the Witness is the Spirit of Christ Himself: when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ, and the glory that should follow (1 Peter 1:11). The Old Testament writers were not guessing about a coming figure; the Spirit within them gave evidence in advance. Hebrews can cite a psalm simply as testimony without naming the human author: But one in a certain place testified, saying, What is man, that thou art mindful of him? (Hebrews 2:6). And the ransom itself is spoken of as evidence entered at the appointed hour: Who gave himself a ransom for all, to be testified in due time (1 Timothy 2:6).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines TESTIFIED as borne witness to; affirmed or declared solemnly, as under oath; given evidence of; and, in the scriptural sense, declared or made known by divine revelation or by the solemn charge of a prophet.

expand to see more

TESTIFIED, pp. — Borne witness to; affirmed or declared solemnly, as in a court of justice.

Given evidence of; manifested; made evident by open declaration or by conduct.

Declared with earnest protestation; charged solemnly, as a prophet testifying against a people.

In the scriptural sense, made known by revelation, as the Spirit testifying beforehand of the sufferings of Christ.

From Latin testis, a witness, and facio, to make — the root also of testimony, attest, protest, and testament.

Key Scripture

Acts 18:5 — "And when Silas and Timotheus were come from Macedonia, Paul was pressed in the spirit, and testified to the Jews that Jesus was Christ."

Acts 20:21 — "Testifying both to the Jews, and also to the Greeks, repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ."

1 Peter 1:11 — "Searching what, or what manner of time the Spirit of Christ which was in them did signify, when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ, and the glory that should follow."

Hebrews 2:6 — "But one in a certain place testified, saying, What is man, that thou art mindful of him? or the son of man, that thou visitest him?"

1 Timothy 2:6 — "Who gave himself a ransom for all, to be testified in due time."

Modern Corruption

Modern evangelism has largely replaced testimony to Christ with testimony about the self, so that my testimony now means the story of a life rather than evidence given concerning a Person and His work.

expand to see more

Acts 18:5 and Acts 20:21 define the content of apostolic testimony without ambiguity: that Jesus is the Christ, and repentance toward God with faith toward the Lord Jesus. Neither text contains a word about the speaker’s biography. When testimony shifts to mean the narration of one’s own experience, three things follow. The evidence becomes unfalsifiable and therefore unarguable, which is comfortable but useless. The dramatic conversion outranks the quiet one, so that the man saved at seven has nothing to say. And the hearer is left to judge Christianity by the improvement in a stranger’s life rather than by the resurrection of Christ, which is the evidence Paul actually put forward in 1 Corinthians 15.

The second corruption is the therapeutic reframing of witness as the sharing of lived experience, in which the authority of the account rests on the speaker’s having undergone it and is therefore beyond challenge. Scripture does use experience — the man born blind said one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see — but he said it in defence of a claim about Christ, under interrogation, and he was arguing. The Bible’s witnesses give testimony that can be examined: dates, places, named officials, five hundred brethren at once, most of whom Paul says are still alive. The dictionary keeps the legal sense: a witness is a man whose word is evidence about something outside himself, and the Spirit of Christ testifying beforehand in the prophets (1 Peter 1:11) is the pattern for all Christian witness.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek martureo (G3140), to bear witness; diamarturomai (G1263), to testify solemnly, to charge earnestly; marturia (G3141), testimony; martus (G3144), a witness, whence martyr; Hebrew ud (H5749), to testify, to warn.

expand to see more

Greek martureo (G3140) — to bear witness, to give evidence; the ordinary courtroom verb (John 15:27; 1 John 5:9).

Greek diamarturomai (G1263) — to testify thoroughly, to charge solemnly; Paul’s word in Acts 20:21 and 2 Timothy 4:1.

Greek marturia (G3141) — the testimony given; the word of their testimony by which the saints overcome (Revelation 12:11).

Greek martus (G3144) — a witness; the English martyr, because witnesses so often sealed the evidence with blood.

Hebrew ud (H5749) — to bear witness, to warn repeatedly; thou didst testify against them (Nehemiah 9:34).

Usage

"Testified to the Jews that Jesus was Christ (Acts 18:5) — the content of the evidence given."

"Testifying… repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ (Acts 20:21) — the whole ministry in one clause."

"It testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ (1 Peter 1:11) — prophecy as advance evidence by the Spirit of Christ."
